vulnerabilities.title: STACK_BUFFER_OVERFLOW via gets() with no bounds check and no stack canary

root_cause.description: The vuln() function allocates a 0x70 (112) byte stack buffer at [rbp-0x70] and passes its address to gets(), which reads an unbounded amount of data from stdin until a newline or EOF is encountered. gets() performs no length validation whatsoever — there is no size parameter to the call. The buffer is only 0x70 bytes, but gets() will write as many bytes as the attacker supplies. The saved RBP (at [rbp], offset 0x70 from buffer start) and the return address (at [rbp+8], offset 0x78 = 120 bytes from buffer start) are both within reach of the overflow. Furthermore, the binary has no stack canary (confirmed by checksec: 'No canary found' and the vuln prologue at 0x401205 contains no canary load/check — only 'push rbp; mov rbp,rsp; sub rsp,0x70'). This means the overflow proceeds undetected and the return address can be overwritten with attacker-controlled data. The root cause is the use of gets() (an inherently unsafe function with no bounds checking) on a fixed-size stack buffer, combined with the complete absence of a stack canary to detect the corruption.

affected_objects: stack buffer at [rbp-0x70] in vuln() — 0x70 (112) bytes, the overflow source
saved RBP at [rbp] in vuln() — overwritable at offset 0x70 from buffer start
return address at [rbp+8] in vuln() — overwritable at offset 0x78 (120 bytes) from buffer start

data_flow: main() calls init() then vuln() with no arguments
vuln() prologue: push rbp; mov rbp,rsp; sub rsp,0x70 — allocates 0x70-byte stack frame
vuln() at 0x401211: lea rax,[rbp-0x70] — computes address of stack buffer
vuln() at 0x401215: mov rdi,rax — passes buffer address as first argument to gets()
vuln() at 0x40121d: call gets@plt — gets() reads unbounded stdin input into the 0x70-byte buffer
Attacker input exceeding 0x70 bytes overwrites saved RBP at offset 0x70
Attacker input exceeding 0x78 bytes overwrites return address at offset 0x78
vuln() at 0x401237: leave — restores RSP from corrupted RBP, then pops corrupted saved RBP into RBP
vuln() at 0x401238: ret — pops the overwritten return address into RIP, transferring control

security_check.expected: Input length should be validated against the buffer size (0x70 bytes) before or during the write operation. A stack canary should be present to detect stack buffer overflow before the function returns.
security_check.actual: No length validation is performed. gets() is called directly with the buffer address and no size limit. No stack canary is present in the binary (confirmed by checksec and the vuln prologue). The function epilogue is a plain 'leave; ret' with no canary check.
security_check.missing_or_incorrect: Both the length check and the stack canary are entirely absent. gets() inherently provides no bounds checking — it reads until newline/EOF. The buffer is 0x70 bytes but there is no mechanism to prevent or detect writes beyond this boundary.

vulnerable_operation.operation: unbounded stack buffer write via gets()
vulnerable_operation.expression: gets(rbp-0x70) — writes attacker-controlled stdin data into a 0x70-byte stack buffer with no length limit
vulnerable_operation.target: stack local buffer at [rbp-0x70] in vuln()'s stack frame; overflow reaches saved RBP at [rbp] (offset 0x70) and return address at [rbp+8] (offset 0x78)
vulnerable_operation.size: buffer declared 0x70 (112) bytes; actual write size is unbounded (determined by attacker input length)

impact.reason: The gets() call writes attacker-controlled data beyond the 0x70-byte buffer boundary, corrupting the saved RBP (at offset 0x70) and return address (at offset 0x78) on the stack. This is a direct stack memory corruption: the overflow overwrites adjacent stack memory with attacker-controlled bytes. No canary detects this corruption. Preconditions: attacker must supply more than 0x70 bytes of input via stdin to the vuln() function.

The saved RBP value on the stack is corrupted at offset 0x70 from the buffer start. When 'leave' executes (mov rsp,rbp; pop rbp), the corrupted RBP is popped into RBP, and subsequent stack frame references in caller functions (main) will use a corrupted base pointer, potentially corrupting data accesses. Preconditions: attacker supplies at least 0x71 bytes of input.

When the overwritten return address at offset 0x78 is not a valid executable address, the 'ret' instruction at 0x401238 will transfer control to an invalid location, causing a SIGSEGV. Even with partial overflow (corrupting only saved RBP), the 'leave' instruction can set RSP to an invalid value, causing a crash on subsequent stack access. Preconditions: attacker supplies at least 0x71 bytes (RBP corruption) or 0x79 bytes (return address corruption) of input.

evidence.description: Disassembly confirms gets@plt is called at 0x40121d with rdi = [rbp-0x70] (set at 0x401211 lea rax,[rbp-0x70]; 0x401215 mov rdi,rax). gets() reads unbounded stdin input into the 0x70-byte stack buffer. There is no length parameter to gets() and no bounds check before or after the call.

The vuln prologue is 'push rbp; mov rbp,rsp; sub rsp,0x70' (0x401209-0x40120d) and the epilogue is 'leave; ret' (0x401237-0x401238). There is no stack canary load (no 'mov rax, [fs:0x28]') or canary check (no 'xor rax,[fs:0x28]; jne ...') anywhere in the function. This confirms the overflow will not be detected.

The stack frame is 0x70 bytes (sub rsp,0x70). The buffer starts at [rbp-0x70] (0x401211). The saved RBP is at [rbp] = offset 0x70 from buffer start. The return address is at [rbp+8] = offset 0x78 (120 bytes) from buffer start. Both are overwritable by input exceeding 0x70 bytes.

checksec confirms: 'No canary found', 'NX enabled', 'No PIE (0x400000)', 'Partial RELRO'. The absence of a canary means the stack overflow is undetectable by the runtime. NX prevents direct shellcode execution on the stack but does not prevent the overflow itself.

The 'ret' instruction at 0x401238 pops the return address from [rsp]. After the overflow, [rsp] at the point of ret contains attacker-controlled data (the overwritten return address at offset 0x78 from the buffer). The return address is fully controlled by the attacker after supplying 120 bytes of padding + 8 bytes of target address.

verification_required: Dynamic confirmation that supplying 120 bytes of padding followed by an 8-byte address overwrites the return address and redirects control flow on 'ret' at 0x401238

CET (SHSTK/IBT) runtime enforcement status: if Shadow Stack is enforced at runtime, the return address overwrite would be detected and cause a SIGSEGV before control transfer. This is UNKNOWN from static analysis — ELF marks SHSTK/IBT as enabled but enforcement requires kernel + CPU support

Whether the close(1)/close(2) calls at 0x401227/0x401231 affect the exploitability of post-overflow control flow (they close stdout/stderr but do not prevent the overflow or the return address overwrite itself)

non_vulnerabilities.reason: setvbuf is called with valid FILE* pointers loaded from .bss globals (stdin@0x404070, stdout@0x404060, stderr@0x404080) and constant arguments (0, 2, 0). The mode value 2 = _IONBF is a valid mode. alarm(60) uses a hardcoded constant argument. No attacker-controlled input reaches these calls. No vulnerability in init().

non_vulnerabilities.description: main() calls init() then vuln() with no arguments, returns 0.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: main passes no arguments to init or vuln. The call sequence is fixed. No attacker-controlled data flows through main itself — the vulnerability is entirely within vuln()'s gets() call. main's own stack frame has no buffer and no unsafe operations.

non_vulnerabilities.description: vuln() calls close(1) and close(2) after gets() — closes stdout (fd 1) and stderr (fd 2).
non_vulnerabilities.reason: close() is called with hardcoded constant arguments (edi=1 at 0x401222, edi=2 at 0x40122c). The arguments are not attacker-controlled. The close calls are not themselves vulnerabilities — they are a constraint on post-overflow exploitation (stdout/stderr are unavailable after the overflow), not a memory safety or logic bug.

non_vulnerabilities.description: Binary has no RPATH/RUNPATH; only NEEDED library is libc.so.6.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: While LD_LIBRARY_PATH could theoretically be used to load a malicious libc, this is an environment-level configuration issue, not a vulnerability in the binary itself. The binary does not load any custom or non-standard libraries. There are no dlopen/dlsym calls. This is a standard fact about library resolution order, not a binary vulnerability.

unresolved.description: CET (Shadow Stack / IBT) runtime enforcement status is unknown
unresolved.reason: The ELF GNU_PROPERTY marks SHSTK and IBT as enabled, and checksec reports both as 'Enabled'. However, actual enforcement requires kernel support (CONFIG_X86_CET) and compatible CPU hardware. If Shadow Stack is enforced at runtime, the return address overwrite at 0x401238 would be detected (the shadow stack's copy of the return address would not match), causing a SIGSEGV before control transfer. This would not prevent the stack memory corruption itself (the overflow still happens), but it would prevent control flow hijacking via the corrupted return address.
unresolved.required_next_step: S3 dynamic verification: run the binary under a CET-capable kernel and attempt the overflow to observe whether a shadow stack violation is triggered. If CET is not enforced, the return address overwrite proceeds to control flow redirection.

unresolved.description: ASLR status for libc base address at exploit time
unresolved.reason: ASLR is a kernel/runtime setting. S1 observed libc at 0x7e3deefd5000 in one ldd run, suggesting ASLR is active. The binary itself is No PIE (fixed at 0x400000), so binary addresses are known. But libc addresses vary per run. This affects whether the overflow's impact extends to libc-based targets but does not affect the existence of the stack buffer overflow vulnerability itself.
unresolved.required_next_step: S3/S4 determination: whether a libc leak is needed for exploitation route planning. This is outside S2 scope — S2 confirms the overflow vulnerability regardless of ASLR.
